wiki_excerpt:
Kālidāsa (Sanskrit: कालिदास, "Servant of Kali"; 4th–5th century CE) was a Classical Sanskrit author who is often considered ancient India's greatest poet and playwright. His plays and poetry are primarily based on Hindu Puranas and philosophy. His surviving works consist of three plays, two epic poems and two shorter poems.


Legend
Kalidasa was once a simple cowherd. Ridiculed as a dimwit, he was tricked into marrying a smart princess; some versions say she was the princess of Kalinga (roughly present-day coastal Orissa), and others, of Ujjayinī (present-day Ujjain). However, very soon after their marriage, she realized that her husband was, in fact, a complete fool, entirely devoid of any learning.
Unable to bear his wife’s mockery, Kalidasa left home and headed straight for a temple of Goddess Kali (Bhadrakāli).
It was well known that if any human ventured there at night, one of two things would happen: either the Goddess’s attendants—the bhutas—would tear the intruder to pieces, or the Goddess herself might be pleased and grant a blessing. Kalidasa went there, prepared for whatever might come. Upon his arrival, he found that the Goddess was away, and the temple stood open. A fool as he was, Kalidasa entered, closed the door, bolted it from the inside, and sat down.
After a while, the Goddess returned. Finding the temple locked, she asked, "Who is inside?" Without opening the door, Kalidasa boldly replied, "Who is outside?" Since it was essential for her to enter before the arrival of other humans, the Goddess hurriedly answered, "Kali is outside." Kalidasa immediately replied, "Then, your *dāsa* (servant) is inside." Pleased by this, the Goddess said, "Kālidāsā! What do you desire? Open the door." Hearing this, Kalidasa replied, "It is vidyā (knowledge) that I seek. I shall not open the door unless you grant me that." The Goddess then instructed, "Stick your tongue out through the gap in the door." As Kalidasa complied, the Goddess used her shula (trident)—or, by some accounts, her fingernails—to inscribe the Chintāmani Mantra—a mantra that bestows profound wisdom—upon his tongue. Instantly, the impurities obscuring Kalidasa’s intellect vanished, much like clouds parting to reveal the clear, radiant light of the moon; he was transformed into a great scholar and a supreme poet.
Kalidasa immediately opened the door, approached the Goddess, and—reciting verses composed on the spot—prostrated himself at her feet. (The hymn Shyamala Dandakam, composed by Kalidasa in praise of the Goddess, is said to have originated from this moment.) The Goddess then returned to the inner sanctum of the temple and resumed her original form. Kalidasa offered his salutations once more before departing. It was when the Goddess, pleased with him, called out, "Kalidasa!" that he came to be known by that name; prior to this, he had been called by a different name.
Upon returning home, having attained profound scholarship through the grace of Kali, his wife asked him, "Asti kaścit vāgarthah?" ("have you attained true, manifest wisdom?"). Kalidasa expressed his deep regard for his wife by incorporating these very words at the beginning of three of his literary works. These works begin with these three terms. Kumārasambhava starts with the word asti ("astyuttarasyām..."), Meghadūta with kaścit ("kaścit kāntāvirahaguruṇā..."), and Raghuvamśa with vāgarthah ("vāgarthāviva sampṛktau...").


Biography

Little is known about Kalidasa's life, except what is inferred from his poetry and plays. His works cannot be dated with precision, but they were most likely authored before the 5th century CE during the Gupta era.


Birthplace
Based on geographical descriptions found in Kalidasa's works, various theories have been put forward placing his birthplace in Bengal, Kashmir, Vidarbha, and Malava (Dashapura, Vidisha, or Ujjayini).
